title: Pauri 24, sound: ant na siftee
hook: ant na siftee kahan na ant
tomorrow: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ant who remembers. Your line was be the ant. Did one small moment become a reminder? Today, a word that sounds just like it and means something else entirely. Day two hundred one.

Here's a small gift from language. Yesterday the hero was an ant. Today, the first word of Pauri 24 is also ant, spelled the same in English letters. But in Punjabi, ant means end. The finish, the limit, the last page. And this stanza is going to use that word again and again, only to say there isn't one. No end, no end, no end. It's as if the whole stanza is a song about a road with no last mile. Today, just its first line, and the sound of it.
screen: `YESTERDAY, AN ANT.` → `TODAY, ANT MEANS END.` → `NO END, NO END, NO END.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 24 in the original: ant na siftee kahan na ant. Let's take it word by word. Ant, with a short a, UNT: end, limit. Na: no, not. Siftee, SIF-tee: praises, qualities. It comes from sifat, an Arabic word that traveled through Persian, meaning an attribute, a quality worthy of praise. Sikhs speak of sifat salaah, praise and glory. Kahan: saying, telling. So: there's no end to the praises, and no end to the telling of them. Now listen to how the line is shaped. It starts with ant and ends with ant. The word for end is at both ends, like two bookends, and between them the line says there's no end. The shape of the sentence plays against its meaning. That's poetry that works even before the meaning arrives. The rest of the stanza keeps going the same way, in paraphrase: no end to His works, no end to His giving, no end to seeing, no end to hearing. Line after line, the word ant, and the word na. Guru Nanak is generally described as writing in the everyday speech of his region rather than a classical language, and his words draw on many sources: Punjabi, words from Sanskrit, words from Persian and Arabic, like sifat here. Tomorrow we'll open what the whole stanza means. Today, the sound. Ant na siftee, kahan na ant. End at both ends, and no end in the middle.
screen: `ANT — END, LIMIT.` · `SIFTEE — PRAISES, QUALITIES.` · `ANT AT BOTH ENDS OF THE LINE.` · `WORDS FROM MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `ANT NA SIFTEE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: ant na siftee, kahan na ant. Feel it start and finish on the same word. Say it twice more, slower. Then sit, and notice the breath. Each breath ends, and another begins, and there's no last one you can feel coming. Rest in that rolling, one breath after another. The bell holds the time.
Siftee, praises. It opens ant na siftee, kahan na ant: no end to the praises, no end to their telling. Ant means end.
Your line: ant na siftee. Today, when something good ends, a meal, a song, a talk, whisper the line, and notice what keeps going. Day two hundred one.

howItsDone: Pauri 24 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its repeated word ant, end, gives the stanza a steady, rolling rhythm that many Sikhs know by heart.

what a scholar hears: ant, end, from Sanskrit anta; siftee from Arabic sifat, attribute; the line is framed by the word it denies.

notes: The English ant / Punjabi ant wordplay is a listener aid only; confirm it's acceptable.
Etymologies: ant < Sanskrit anta; sifat < Arabic via Persian. Confirm.

Statement that Guru Nanak wrote in spoken languages and borrowed from Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic is general; confirm. Reviewer softened it to 'generally described as', since scholars differ on how to name the language of Japji (Old Punjabi, Sant Bhasha, a mixed idiom).

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the overclaim that sifat salaah is heard 'all through Sikh life'; sifat's origin stated plainly (Arabic via Persian); 'poetry you can feel' no longer tells the listener what they feel.
